newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government aims to simplify market rules.
newsitem.headline: German government aims to simplify market rules.

text.p: Germany plans to simplify stock market regulatory reporting rules for foreign firms and improve conditions for raising capital in hopes of wooing more firms to Germany's capital markets, a senior government official said.

The German government is also gearing up for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 with a comprehensive legal framework for the euro, Juergen Stark, state secretary for the finance ministry, said on Thursday at a news conference to launch draft capital markets legislation.

The role of Germany as a financial centre after currency union, targeted for January 1 1999, is a hot topic in a country which has long lived in London's shadow but believes it is set to take on new importance when EMU becomes reality.
Gaining access to capital markets has to be made easier, Stark said, while investor confidence has to be boosted at the same time.
Lawmakers can only improve the legislative conditions, while banks and bourses had to motivate citizens to invest in shares and other securities, Stark said.
Stark said he would be tightening up the rules on regulatory reporting for German listed companies.

Under the third phase of legislation to promote German financial markets, which is due to become law on January 1, 1998, German companies will have to report facts relating to either their financial situation or their asset position.
Up until now, companies have only had to report facts which affect both their financial position and their asset position.
A loosening of reporting requirements for foreign companies was necessary, Stark said.
Many foreign companies had problems with the rule which required them to report any planned ad-hoc statements to both the German securities watchdog (BaWe) and the German bourse.

In order to avoid difficulties with regulators in both their domicile countries and in Germany, many companies were simply not bothering to examine the German capital markets as an option, Stark said.
"This is not in the interest of Germany as a financial centre," Stark said.
